1. The animation shows a homeowner, Tessa, comparing two mortgage options. One is a 15-year payment of $2,828 a month. The other is a 30-year mortgage, where she pays $2,948 a month, which is $120 more, so the loan is paid off in 15 years. This is an "illustrative" example based on Freddie Mac survey rates.

2. In frame 1 the 30-year bar drops slightly, with a "fallback" label. In frames 2 and 3, the monthly figures appear and a small gold "+$120 a month" slice sits on top of the green 30-year bar. In frames 4 and 5, gold slices fall off the bar into a pile of coins. In frame 6 the pile has grown into a stack labeled "$21,622 extra paid over 15 years."

3. Paying the 30-year loan on a 15-year schedule costs about $120 more per month than the actual 15-year loan. Over 15 years that adds up to roughly $21,622 in extra payments. The "fallback" label in frame 1 likely refers to the option of dropping back to the lower 30-year payment if needed. The footer says it is US only, and "history, not a forecast."

4. The animation gives little direct advice. A viewer would probably take away that the 15-year loan has a lower monthly payment than a 30-year loan prepaid on the same schedule, so the 30-year loan costs more in total. A viewer might also notice that the 30-year loan keeps a lower required payment as a fallback.

5. The animation only suggests this through its picture and numbers, and it never gives an explicit instruction. My reading of the "fallback" label and the $21,622 stack is my own conclusion. The text says nothing about whether to prepay or invest.
